candidateRows: The freedom grounding moral responsibility is compatible with determinism, while libertarian or indeterminist freedom is an expendable fantasy.
This directly defines the compatibilist side of the motion and distinguishes responsibility-preserving freedom from the libertarian conception both speakers reject.
Harris's published characterization of Dennett's compatibilism as mistaken or quasi-theological.
After discussing their contentious written exchange, Dennett argues that Harris already accepts determinism-compatible responsibility and is therefore close to compatibilism.
Ordinary free agency consists in the competence to undertake obligations and act responsibly, capacities that depend on a functioning nervous system rather than indeterminism.
The move supplies concrete criteria for the compatibilist freedom at issue and explains why some agents possess it while impaired agents may not.
Dennett moves from broad agreement about naturalism to contracts, promises, disability, and nervous-system competence as practical markers of responsible agency.
Compatibilism legitimately preserves a naturalistic concept of free will by discarding inherited magical commitments rather than accepting traditional usage as decisive.
This explains the conceptual method behind Dennett's position and answers the charge that revising free will amounts to theology or doctrinal evasion.
Harris's request for Dennett to state compatibilism and address Harris's earlier theological characterization.
Asked to define compatibilism, Dennett compares free will with consciousness and argues that naturalistic conceptual revision can preserve a real phenomenon without its magical interpretation.
Compatibilism risks changing the subject when it removes features that are integral to the concept people mean by free will rather than merely correcting incidental folk beliefs.
The objection targets whether compatibilist freedom answers the original free-will problem at all, making it a direct challenge to the opposing side's central definition.
Dennett's claim that free will can be retained after its mysterious or magical interpretation is discarded.
Harris accepts that concepts can be purified but distinguishes legitimate explanation from eliminating core features and then applying the original label to a different phenomenon.
Freedom is the controlled possession of many practical degrees of action, especially the sophisticated capacity to be moved by reasons, not exemption from determinism.
The move offers Dennett's positive core account of free will and places reasons-responsive control, rather than causal indeterminacy, at the center of the motion.
Harris's contention that compatibilism changes the subject by eliminating the concept's allegedly ineliminable core.
Dennett rejects a sharp boundary between clarification and subject change, then uses engineering degrees of freedom to explain the distinctive versatility and control of human agents.
Responsible agency is a graded package of beliefs, ordered desires, attention, reasons-responsiveness, and self-control whose presence distinguishes free from unfree agents regardless of determinism.
This operationalizes reasons-responsive freedom, identifies how it can be impaired or usurped, and connects the resulting classification directly to moral responsibility.
Using a defective chess program and the model of a trustworthy adult, Dennett argues that freedom depends on available capacities and their control, not on the causal structure of the universe.

Compatibilism neglects the first-person authorship and ability-to-do-otherwise experience that motivates the free-will problem, replacing the mythical object of concern with an agreed but different reality.
The move states Harris's principal case against compatibilism: its useful capacities do not answer the subjective libertarian claim whose falsity makes free will problematic.
Dennett's reasons-responsive account of responsible agency and claim that determinism is irrelevant to distinguishing free and unfree agents.

Harris contrasts third-person capacities with the felt authorship of thoughts and choices, denies that an identical rewind permits another action, and likens compatibilist preservation to renaming Sicily as Atlantis.

Naturalistic freedom preserves the responsibility-relevant distinctions people need, and deliberating agents require an actionable sense of open alternatives without requiring magical or exact-replay alternatives.
This directly answers Harris's phenomenological objection by explaining both why nonmagical freedom matters and how meaningful alternative possibilities function within deterministic agency.
Harris's claim that people's real concern is libertarian authorship and that compatibilism substitutes a different phenomenon.
Dennett concedes that magical freedom does not exist but argues that agents must treat some matters as open, and that nearby-world variation can justify saying an agent could have acted otherwise.

Even tiny physical contingencies governing major choices undermine the ordinary felt picture of autonomous personhood by revealing the agent as dependent on causal factors outside conscious authorship.
The move presses the psychological and metaphysical consequence Harris thinks remains after accepting Dennett's nearby-alternatives account: conscious agency still lacks ultimate authorship.
Dennett's deterministic chess example and claim that small nearby changes justify saying an agent could have done otherwise.
Harris argues that a synaptic charge or similarly minute condition could redirect an entire life, reviving the image of marionette strings even though no external puppeteer exists.
Absolute indeterminacy would not create free will, while reasons-responsive determination can support responsibility because different choices require changes proportionate to the balance of reasons.
The response rejects indeterminacy as a solution and begins a positive account linking responsible choice to deliberative reasons and robust determination rather than causal randomness.
Harris's argument that sensitivity to tiny physical differences restores marionette strings and subverts ordinary personhood.

Dennett distinguishes genuine toss-ups from decisions where reasons strongly favor one side, then invokes the libertarian demand for an undetermined choice and Luther's responsible declaration that he could do no other.
Even small neural variations can determine consequential actions, so chance is not confined to decisions already balanced on a knife-edge.
This challenges Dennett's effort to quarantine indeterminacy to close decisions by arguing that tiny differences can transform lives through ordinary actions.
Dennett's claim that microscopic variation matters chiefly when a decision is already a genuine toss-up.
After Dennett argues that random resolution of close choices does not undermine responsibility, Harris contends that minute causal differences can govern highly consequential actions.
Libertarian free will is incoherent under determinism and indeterminism alike, whereas Dennett preserves other valued capacities by redefining the term.
The move directly defines the debate's fundamental disagreement: whether to reject free will as nonexistent or retain a compatibilist reconstruction of it.
Dennett's proposal to retain a graded, practical kind of freedom grounded in lawful and effective agency.
Following Dennett's discussion of regret and self-control, Harris says they agree against libertarianism but diverge over whether the name free will should survive.
Complete neurophysiological understanding would exculpate ordinary wrongdoing in the same basic way that Charles Whitman's brain tumor appears exculpatory.
The argument supplies Harris's central bridge from exceptional neurological impairment to universal causal non-authorship and diminished ultimate responsibility.
Dennett's contention that responsible agents remain accountable despite incomplete control over how their decisions are produced.
Harris uses the case of a mass shooter with a brain tumor to argue that ordinary synaptic causes are likewise unauthored and therefore similarly exculpatory.
Neuroscience shows that human beings are causally wired, not that everyone is wired wrongly or disabled in a responsibility-destroying way.
This defends the compatibilist distinction between ordinary competent agency and genuine impairment against Harris's universal exculpation argument.
Harris's argument that full causal understanding makes every person's conduct analogous to behavior caused by a brain tumor.
Dennett grants that Whitman was impaired but rejects the inference that everyone is similarly disabled, grounding responsibility in sufficient rather than perfect ability.
Differences in practical capacity remain real, but nobody authors the genes, environment, or prior brain states that produce those capacities and choices.
The move answers compatibilism at its strongest point by accepting reasons-responsive differences while denying that they establish ultimate moral authorship.
Dennett's claim that adequate ability and normal wiring distinguish responsible agents from people with exculpatory impairments.
Harris accepts voluntary-control distinctions but argues that genes and environment exhaust their causal basis, using Saddam Hussein's development to illustrate pervasive luck.
Control does not require controlling every background condition; it consists in competently responding to uncontrolled conditions and maintaining self-governance.
This provides the affirmative compatibilist model of agency: bounded control can be genuine, cultivated, socially consequential, and sufficient for practical responsibility.
Harris's inference from our lack of control over genes and environment to the absence of genuine authorship and responsibility.
Dennett argues that sailors and control systems genuinely control outcomes without controlling every input, then applies that model to moral education and autonomous adulthood.
A highly competent agent's rare lapse appears maximally blameworthy yet least expressive of that agent, exposing a tension between competence and responsible authorship.
The example pressures competence-based responsibility by arguing that the rarer and less characteristic a lapse is, the more salient luck becomes in explaining it.
Dennett's claim that cultivated competence and reliable self-control ground genuine practical responsibility for an adult's conduct.
Harris compares an expert golfer's extraordinary miss with a moral lapse, arguing that exceptional competence can make the failure less representative of the person.
Greater competence can increase responsibility because others reasonably rely on it, and apparent bad luck may reflect correctable failures in self-management.
This directly answers the competence paradox by grounding heightened accountability in undertaken obligations, justified reliance, and the agent's capacity for improvement.
Harris's claim that a rare lapse by the most competent agent is least expressive of that agent and therefore most attributable to luck.
Dennett compares elite competence to a trusted official's obligations, arguing that reliance heightens accountability and that inquiry may uncover avoidable contributors to failure.
Tracing an anomalous lapse to earlier choices does not restore authorship, because each earlier choice is itself another causally produced and unauthored event.
The recursive argument blocks attempts to relocate responsibility to an earlier avoidable choice and supports preserving accountability without ultimate self-authorship.
Dennett's suggestion that investigation can connect an anomalous lapse to avoidable prior conduct and failures of self-management.
Harris argues that a radically uncharacteristic act says little about the prior person and that citing earlier conduct merely moves the unauthored causal problem backward.
People can author themselves within limits and sustain moral agency by accepting community standards and responsibility even when luck contributes to failure.
This states the compatibilist alternative to absolute self-creation and explains why causal luck does not nullify an agent's standing commitment to accountability.
Harris's claim that nobody truly authors themselves and that accountability can be retained without preserving that alleged illusion.
Dennett concedes limits and luck while maintaining that people construct themselves from available materials and properly accept responsibility as members of a moral community.
Complete causal information would show that responsibility for a performance failure is only a practical heuristic, not genuine authorship of the failure.
The move directly separates socially useful responsibility practices from the deeper authorship that Harris argues causal explanation undermines.
Dennett's claim that agents remain responsible despite the constitutive role of luck.
After Dennett treats appeals to cosmic bad luck as irrelevant to responsible agency, Harris argues that fuller causal knowledge exposes responsibility as a practical convention.
Responsibility need not be absolute because free will and legal accountability are pragmatic, consequentialist institutions calibrated to human capacities.
This supplies the compatibilist standard of responsibility and explains why pragmatic, nonmetaphysical accountability can remain real and socially indispensable.
Harris's claim that causally explained conduct leaves only a heuristic attribution of responsibility.
Dennett answers the Tiger Woods example by rejecting absolute responsibility as the relevant benchmark and grounding responsibility in reasonable, evolved legal practices.
Even if pathological wrongdoing were curable, predictable punishment would remain necessary because deterrence and public confidence depend on stable, enforceable rules.
The argument explains why causal diagnosis and treatment do not displace responsibility practices, since their effects extend beyond rehabilitation of one offender.
Harris's anti-Madoff-pill example suggesting that causal understanding and cure would exculpate offenders.
Responding to the proposed cure for Madoff-like conduct, Dennett broadens the analysis to incentives, mutual expectations, legal legitimacy, and institutional stability.
Practical punishment may influence behavior, but complete causal understanding would reveal every action and reaction as an unchosen brain state rather than self-authorship.
The move directly states Harris's central distinction between useful social regulation and the first-person authorship that causal neuroscience would undermine.
Dennett's argument that punishment and stable legal expectations preserve responsible moral agency.
Harris accepts many practical features of punishment but argues that greater causal knowledge would assimilate wrongdoing and ordinary responses to treatable neurological conditions.
Behavioral prediction does not by itself refute free will, because prediction has theoretical and contextual limits and predictable competent reasoning can still be agency.
This directly contests the alleged inference from advance neural predictability to lost agency and reframes predictability as context-sensitive rather than intrinsically undermining.
Harris's claim that advance prediction of thoughts and actions would shatter experienced authorship.
Dennett challenges both current neuroscience's predictive power and the philosophical force of prediction, arguing that ordinary predictable competence is not thereby unfree.
Conscious authorship operates through temporally extended, high-level control and does not require awareness or control of the microprocess generating every action.
The move provides a positive compatibilist model of authorship in which planning, training, and high-level control suffice despite unconscious implementation details.
Harris's suggestion that neural access to words before conscious awareness defeats authorship.
Dennett argues that artists and athletes legitimately author performances by shaping and training underlying processes even when individual outputs arise before focal awareness.
Compatibilism understates the first-person loss involved in rejecting libertarian freedom because people care about an actual ability to have done otherwise.
This identifies the disputed conception of freedom and argues that shared rejection of libertarianism has greater psychological consequences than compatibilism acknowledges.
Dennett's macro-level account of authorship through trained and controlled processes.
After Dennett defends artistic and athletic authorship, Harris argues that ordinary people value a stronger first-person ability to have acted differently in the same situation.
An agent could have done otherwise when possessing competence across a range of actions, without requiring atom-for-atom replay of the identical physical universe.
The move directly defends the compatibilist meaning of alternative possibilities against the deterministic replay criterion central to Harris's objection.
Harris's assertion that both speakers must ultimately agree nobody could have done otherwise.
Dennett answers Harris by grounding alternatives in an agent's real competencies and dismissing exact physical duplication as irrelevant to ordinary causal possibility.
Deterministic processes can still instantiate genuine randomness and meaningful alternatives when outcomes lack a salient cause and vary under relevantly similar conditions.
The coin-flip analysis supplies a concrete compatibilist account of randomness and could-have-done-otherwise that does not depend on metaphysical indeterminism.
Harris's claim that capacity only supports doing otherwise next time, not having done otherwise then.
Following Harris's replay objection, Dennett argues that exact deterministic repetition does not erase the useful causal distinction between open random processes and controlled outcomes.
Neither deterministic chaos nor practical randomization gives agents upstream ownership, while sufficiently early neural prediction would produce a compelling sense of marionette-like nonauthorship.
This restates the central incompatibilist objection: randomness cannot create authorship, and conscious experience does not originate the causal processes producing action.
Dennett's claim that deterministic coin flips realize genuine randomness and meaningful alternatives.
Harris grants the usefulness of chaotic randomizers but argues that people lack ownership of their causes and would experience prior neural prediction as a direct threat to authorship.
The distinction between deterministic chaos and quantum indeterminacy makes no moral difference and is not a cheap substitute for allegedly real randomness.
The claim directly supports compatibilism by denying that metaphysical indeterminacy supplies any morally relevant freedom unavailable in a deterministic world.
Harris's characterization of coin-flip randomness as merely a surrogate for true randomness and of prediction as threatening authorship.
After Harris argues that complete advance prediction would produce a marionette-like loss of authorship, Dennett disputes the implied downgrade of deterministic randomness.
The contrast between deterministic chaos and quantum indeterminacy was offered only as a distinction between physical facts, not as a source of moral difference.
The clarification preserves Harris's argument from being treated as dependent on quantum indeterminacy having special moral significance.
Dennett's response that deterministic chaos and quantum indeterminacy make no moral difference.
Dennett has just argued that the two physical regimes are morally equivalent; Harris narrows his prior point to a physical distinction alone.
People are mistaken to think they need libertarian free will because the forms of free will worth wanting are fully compatible with determinism.
This is the compatibilist thesis at the center of the motion: worthwhile human freedom does not require exemption from deterministic causation.
Harris's insistence that the libertarian sense of authorship is psychologically important even though people lack that freedom.
Following agreement that quantum indeterminacy adds no moral difference, Dennett concludes that libertarian expectations are delusive and unnecessary.
